content: The relevant actions should be determined based on the date when the early response activities were completed. For cases such as Ebola virus disease, the notification date is defined as the date when a clinician or a facility’s surveillance focal point contacted the public health department or local surveillance officer to report a suspected case of viral hemorrhagic fever. If the case was detected but no contact was made with public health authorities, and the authorities only became aware of the suspected case upon receiving laboratory results, the notification date is the date when the public health authorities received the laboratory result. If an event was detected by a community health worker and directly reported to a surveillance officer or public health department, the notification date is the date of that report. If the community health worker reported the event to a health facility, the notification date is the date when the health facility subsequently reported the event to the surveillance officer or public health department. For events detected by a central media-scanning unit or an event-based surveillance program, the notification date is the date when the central unit or program notified the public health authorities at the jurisdictional level responsible for investigating or responding to the event. For events identified through aggregated indicator-based surveillance, the notification date is the date when the analyst or surveillance officer informed a team member responsible for investigating or ensuring a public health response. In addition to the date when early response activities were completed, it is recommended to also review the date when the early response was initiated. This refers to the date when the first of the seven early response actions was completed. While the initiation date is not used to calculate the 7-1-7 metrics, it is valuable for identifying bottlenecks that may have delayed the response initiation. The goal should be to initiate the early response within one day of notification. The early response actions outlined in the guidance emphasize the initiation rather than the completion of a response. They provide a framework to ensure that the relevant pillars of a response, as detailed in other guidance and tools, have been activated. These actions serve as simple indicators, refined through pilot testing, to identify the dates when specific actions were taken. Some countries have found that expanding early response actions into event-related or disease-specific job aids, which detail specific activities, improves performance and accountability. For example, initiating appropriate risk communication and community engagement activities includes: The date when a local or public health official announced the outbreak. The date when messaging to reduce risk or prevent spread was published or communicated. The date when two-way dialogue with communities was initiated. The date when community sentiment or knowledge, attitudes, or perceptions of the event were assessed. Establishing a coordination mechanism includes: The date when an incident management system was activated. The date when the emergency operations center was activated. The date when a task force or technical working group was convened. The date when an incident action plan was drafted. IPC (infection prevention and control) measures should also be considered as part of the response framework.
